# Grundlage

Zero-dependency library for building web components with tagged template literals.
Server-rendered and hydrated on the client. `npm install grundlage`.

## Mental model

A component is a generator function passed to `component`, the component BODY. It runs ONCE
when the element mounts and runs to completion (never `while (true)`). It yields exactly three
kinds of value:

- an `html` TEMPLATE paints once and stays until the next template or update generator
  replaces it;
- an UPDATE GENERATOR, `yield function* view() { … }`, runs now and again on every update,
  and the previous run is torn down before the next one starts. `view` is only a name for the
  reader, not a keyword: any name, or none (`yield function* () { … }`), behaves the same;
- a PROMISE waits: the `yield` evaluates to its value, and a rejection throws at the `yield`.

Data the SERVER should fetch for the first paint comes through one helper, WITH the star:
`const user = yield* load(() => fetchUser(id))` (see API).

Anything else throws, `async` included: there is no `async function*`, no arrow render function
and no `await`. The body's ONE argument is a props object carrying `host` plus every prop
declared in `component(gen, { props })`, and an update generator receives the same object. A
`yield` of a template evaluates back to the host element. A `yield` of an update generator WAITS
until a run of it finishes and evaluates to what that run returned. A returned function is the
cleanup. There are no signals and no hooks. An update happens on `host.update()`, on
`host.setProp(…)`, on assigning a declared prop to a NEW value, and when a DECLARED attribute on
the host element changes. An undeclared attribute (`class`, `style`, `data-*`) does not trigger
an update. A template BINDING the host's own declared prop to a new value triggers one too (see
Host attributes). An update re-runs the update generator; the component body itself does not
re-run, so state declared in the body survives updates because the update generator closes over
it.

## Complete example

```javascript
import { component, html } from "grundlage";

// the schema is a plain object; hoisting it keeps the element's inputs readable at a glance
// (in TypeScript this needs `satisfies Schema`, see Rules)
const props = { start: [Number, 0], label: [String, "count"] };

customElements.define(
	"click-counter",
	component(
		function* ({ host, start }) {
			let count = start; // `start` is a SEED: the generator body runs once

			const increment = () => {
				count += 1;
				host.update(); // re-runs the update generator below; count is still here
			};

			// destructured in the update generator, so `label` is LIVE, re-read every update
			yield function* view({ label }) {
				yield html`<button onClick=${increment}>${label}: ${count}</button>`;
			};
		},
		{ props },
	),
);
```

Waiting inside an update generator paints a placeholder first, and an update while it waits
starts over:

```javascript
yield function* view({ userId }) {
	yield html`<p>Loading…</p>`;
	const user = yield fetchUser(userId);
	yield html`<p>${user.name}</p>`;
};
```

## API

`component(generator, options?) => CustomElementConstructor`
  Register the return value with `customElements.define`. The first argument MUST be a
  generator function (`function*`). A plain, arrow or `async` function throws a
  `TypeError` at definition time, not at mount. `options` extends `ShadowRootInit`; the
  defaults are `{ mode: "open", clonable: true, delegatesFocus: true, serializable: true }`
  and any option passed overrides its default. `options.props` is the SCHEMA (see below):
  it fixes the observed attributes and installs one accessor per prop on the element class.
  `formAssociated: true` swaps the base class for the form-associated one. `{ mode: "closed" }`
  still hydrates and reuses `load` results: the closed root is reached through
  `attachInternals().shadowRoot` instead of `host.shadowRoot`, so server output is reused
  rather than painted again. The return value is a class. `class extends component(fn) {}` is
  the extension point for methods, getters and static fields; nothing is assigned to `host`
  at runtime.

`options.props`, the schema
  `{ propName: entry }`, where an entry is a FUNCTION taking whatever arrived and returning
  the value, or `undefined` to REFUSE it:
  `(incoming) => incoming instanceof Quote ? incoming : undefined`. `String`, `Number`, `BigInt` and `Boolean` are shorthands for the
  four shipped functions. `[entry, fallback]` supplies what the function is called with when
  nothing was supplied. That is the whole schema. There is no separate optional or required
  shape, and no type guard: a prop is its function.

  The function is the ONE place a value is parsed or validated, and it serves the attribute
  and the property mode. A string means the value came from markup and needs parsing; anything
  else came from JS and is already itself:
  `(incoming) => typeof incoming === "string" ? incoming.split(" ") : incoming`.

  Five rules cover the whole model:

  1. ONE VALUE PER PROP, in one store the element owns. Last write wins, whichever mode it
     came from, and nothing is compared across modes.
  2. EVERY INCOMING VALUE runs through the prop's function: markup, a property assignment, a
     parent's binding, `setProp`, the fallback at construction.
  3. A REFUSAL IS IGNORED. The previous value stays and the console warns; nothing throws and
     nothing updates.
  4. ABSENCE IS A WRITE OF THE FALLBACK. `removeAttribute`, `el.x = undefined`, `el.x = null`
     and element construction are one code path, so NOTHING is required and no read fails.
     The fallback is not restored: the function is asked the same question and gives the same
     answer, whenever it is asked.
  5. A PROPERTY ASSIGNMENT REFLECTS when the value it settled on has a string spelling. An
     attribute arriving from markup does not: `count="007"` stays as written while `el.count`
     reads `7`.

  Every prop observes an attribute: the LOWERCASED prop name. `userId` observes `userid`,
  and either spelling binds in markup. Prop names must match `/^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*$/` and
  two props differing only in case throw at define time. Every declared prop becomes an
  accessor on the element class, so a name already on the prototype chain (`title`, `id`,
  `lang`, `hidden`, `update`, `setProp`, `internals`) throws at define time, as does `host`,
  which the props object reserves, and any name starting with `on-`, which markup reads as a
  custom event binding.

  A fallback is COPIED per element with `structuredClone` for anything object-shaped (deeply:
  a nested object is a fresh one too), and SHARED for a primitive, a function and a
  `Template`. A value `structuredClone` cannot reproduce (a class instance, an object
  holding a function) throws at define time and names the remedy: put the default inside the
  function, `(incoming) => incoming ?? new Value()`, which runs once per element. So does a
  fallback the prop's own function refuses; the check calls the function once, before any
  element exists.

  Reflection writes the value's own spelling: a string as itself, a number or bigint through
  `String(value)`, `true` as `""`. A value with no spelling (an object, `undefined`) takes a
  stale attribute OFF and touches nothing when there was none. `false` removes the attribute
  too, unless absence for that prop reads `true` (`[Boolean, true]`), where removing would
  say the opposite and it writes `"false"` instead. Reading is symmetric: `x`, `x=""` and
  `x="true"` are `true`, `x="false"` is `false`.

  The type layer sees the shape, not the function: a bare entry is `T | undefined`, and a
  `[entry, fallback]` is `T`. The visible fallback is the only way to promise a value. A
  bare `Boolean` is the exception, typed `boolean`, since absence is one of its two states.
  The fallback ITSELF is not type-checked against the entry: a wrong one is a define-time
  throw with a readable message rather than a compile error.

`` html`...` `` => `Template` (opaque)
  Tagged template literal. Each distinct literal is parsed once and cached (keyed by its
  strings array); later paints only touch dynamic parts. Yield it, or embed it inside
  another `html` template.

`props(element, schema) => typed object`
  The same schema, read once from a plain `HTMLElement` that never went through `component`,
  or for reading something deliberately left unobserved. NOT the primary spelling: a
  component declares its props in `component(gen, { props })` and receives them as its one
  argument. The returned object is a SNAPSHOT; the schema is normalized once per schema object,
  so hoist it rather than writing it inline at the call. An own property under the prop name
  wins over the attribute (case intact: `element.userTags`, not `usertags`); with neither, the
  prop's function answers absence. A value the function refuses warns and reads as absent, the
  same as everywhere else. The export collides with the conventional `const props = {…}`
  schema name, so a module using both renames one (`import { props as readProps }`).

`yield* load(fetcher)` and `yield* load(key, fetcher)` => the fetcher's awaited result
  Data needed before the first paint:

  ```javascript
  const user = yield* load(() => fetchUser(userId));
  const stats = yield* load("stats", () => fetchStats());
  ```

  ALWAYS with the star, and NO `host` argument: `load()` returns a generator, the star types
  the result as the fetcher's, and `yield load(…)` throws. The fetcher returns a value or a
  promise. On the server it runs and the result is written into the shadow root as a
  `<script type="application/json" data-ssr>`. While the browser HYDRATES that markup, the
  same `load` returns the server's result and removes the script instead of fetching.
  Everywhere else (a client-only mount, every later run) the fetcher runs. There is no
  `skipSSR` and no options object.

  Unkeyed loads take the server's results in ORDER, per element, so a `load` inside a branch
  the server and the browser can take differently needs a string KEY. A mixin builds its key
  from its arguments, `` load(`user-${id}`, …) ``, because a key used twice in one element
  throws on the server. The result crosses as JSON: return plain objects, arrays, strings,
  finite numbers, booleans or `null`. A `Date`, a `Map`, a class instance, a `Response`, a
  bigint or a template throws and names the fix. A fetcher that fails on the server throws
  at the `yield*`, where a `try/catch` can paint a fallback, and the browser runs that load
  again. The body runs once, so a `load` there runs once; inside an update generator a
  `load` runs on every update.

`host.update() => Promise<void>`
  The update trigger. See Rules for what it re-fires and when it resolves. On the server an
  update asked for during the paint (a host binding writing an own prop, a synchronous
  `update()` or prop assignment inside the update generator) runs before the run ends, so the
  markup shows the settled value; once the run has ended, it is a no-op. On a DISCONNECTED host
  it is a no-op too: it queues nothing and resolves immediately, and a removal settles an
  `update()` that was already pending.

`host.setProp(name, value, oldValue?) => void`
  Imperative counterpart to a markup binding, for a framework/interop driver feeding props
  from outside. A DECLARED name is assigned through its own accessor, so it runs the prop's
  function, reflects and schedules, and `null`/`undefined` is the absence that writes the
  fallback back. An undeclared name resolves the same way a dynamic attribute does:
  stringable → attribute, non-stringable → property, `on*`/`on-*` plus a function → event
  listener. Pass `oldValue` so a previously bound listener is removed; the other mode is
  cleared either way.

`host.internals => ElementInternals | null`
  Lazily attached on first read, on every component, not only form-associated ones. `null`
  on the server.

Types: `BaseComponent`, `Cleanup`, `ComponentOptions`, `ComponentProps`, `DeclaredProps`,
`Resolve`, `Schema`, `Template`, `UpdateGenerator`, `YieldableValue`.

## Bindings

```
content        <p>${text}</p>
attribute      <div class=${className}>
mixed attr     <div class="static ${dynamic}">
event          <button onClick=${handler}>          // on + EventName
custom event   <color-swatch on-swatch-select=${handler}>
spread         <div ${attributes}>                  // object → name/value, array → boolean attrs
list           <ul>${items.map((i) => html`<li>${i}</li>`)}</ul>
list key       <li><!--${item.id}-->…</li>          // first dynamic comment = row identity
nested         <div>${show && html`<details>…</details>`}</div>
dynamic tag    <${tagName}>content</${tagName}>
raw            <style>${css}</style>                // style/script/textarea
comment        <!-- note ${value} -->               // second and later dynamic comments
```

## Host attributes

If the OUTERMOST node of a yielded template is a `<template>` and it has no top-level siblings,
the wrapper is unwrapped: its children become the shadow DOM and its attributes are applied
to the host element. This is how a component sets its own `class`/`id`/`role`/handlers from
the inside.

```javascript
yield function* view({ role }) {
	yield html`<template class="card" role="${role}" on-form-reset=${reset}>…</template>`;
};
```

- Static, dynamic, boolean, multi-part attributes and spreads all work and update between
  paints.
- Event handlers bind here too (e.g. `on-form-*` for form components).
- Attributes dropped by a later paint are reverted on the host.
- A host binding that writes one of the host's OWN declared props is a write like any other: it
  runs the prop's function, reflects, and updates when the value changed, at mount, at
  hydration and on every patch alike. The next paint binds the same value, the change gate
  skips it, and the component settles, so `<template theme=${x}>` with `componentProps.theme`
  painted inside shows `x` in the same frame, at the cost of one extra update generator run. A
  binding derived from the prop itself (`` html`<template count=${componentProps.count + 1}>…`
  ``) never settles: it is the update loop below and ends in a visible error. Derive the bound
  value from something the paint does not write (a local, another prop).
- A `<template>` WITH attributes in a nested position (content hole, list row) throws. A
  `<template>` that has top-level siblings is parsed as an ordinary element instead.

## Lists and keys

An array in a content hole paints one row per entry. Rows are matched by the row template's
identity and a content hash, which covers most reorders and edits without extra work. For
explicit identity, put a dynamic comment in the row: the FIRST dynamic comment of a template
is consumed as its key, never reaches the DOM, and binds that row's DOM (focus, scroll,
input state) to the value. Text around the expression is fine, it is constant across the
rows of one template, so only the expression tells rows apart: `<!--${id}-->` and
`<!-- key: ${id} -->` work the same way.

A row matched to the previous paint is PATCHED when its template is the same literal. A
KEYED row can also be matched ACROSS a template change, since the key is its whole identity
then: that row is rebuilt in place, keeping its position in the list, with new nodes and no
DOM state carried over. An unkeyed row is only ever matched to its own template.

An ITERATOR paints the same as the array it yields: a generator object,
``items.values().map((item) => html`<li>${item}</li>`)``, `map.values()`. It is read once, at
the paint that holds it, so build it inside the update generator: an iterator kept across
paints is used up and paints an empty list the second time. A `Map` or a `Set` itself is not
an iterator.

Row values: string / number / bigint paint as text (`""`, `0`, `NaN` included); `null`,
`undefined`, `true`, `false` paint nothing but still occupy a row; a nested array or iterator
paints recursively; anything else (plain object, `Date`, function, symbol) throws.

## Rules (get these right)

- The component body runs ONCE per mount and runs to completion, no `while (true)`. State
  declared in the body persists across updates (the update generator closes over it), so
  mutable state belongs there rather than being re-derived.
- Don't hang state or methods on `host` (`host.query = …`, `host.close = () => …`). The host
  is not an instance bag. Keep state in generator-local variables, communicate outward by
  dispatching events and inward by reading attributes/props. Real methods come from extending
  the returned class (`class extends component(fn) {}`); a property assigned at runtime only
  exists once `connectedCallback` has run.
- Updates are triggered by `host.update()`, by `host.setProp(…)`, by assigning a declared
  prop a value it did not already hold (`el.items = […]`, `el.label = "x"`), and by a change
  to a DECLARED attribute. A write the prop's function refuses, and a re-write of the same
  primitive, schedule nothing. A component's own host binding writing one of its own props
  schedules like any other write (Host attributes). Undeclared attributes are not observed at
  all. There is no other reactivity.
- `update()` re-runs the update generator the component body yielded LAST: its current run is
  torn down (its `finally` and cleanup run) and the function runs again from the top, in a new
  run. While the body has not yet reached its first update generator, and after the body yields
  a template instead, `update()` is a no-op that resolves at once. The body itself never
  re-runs. A template the body yields after an update generator tears it down and takes the
  shadow root back for good, and a second update generator the body yields replaces the first.
- `await host.update()` resolves once the run it started has run to its END, in a microtask, not
  after the browser paints; there is no rAF in the path. So the awaited state is the settled UI,
  placeholder and all waiting included. An update generator that waits on a promise that never
  settles keeps that `update()` pending until a later run ends, the body yields a template over
  it, or the host is removed. Concurrent `update()` calls coalesce onto the pending pass and
  share its promise.
- Code that runs straight after a `yield` of a template or an update generator sees THIS
  component's own DOM, never the update of a child it just wrote to. The queued children
  update once no generator is left on the stack, and nothing that code can do brings that
  forward: it holds on a mount as on an update, for a child the paint just created as for one
  that was already there, after an update generator whose first run finished without waiting,
  and around a component this code MOUNTS itself, which runs its own generator on the spot and
  still leaves the queue alone. One more `yield` of a promise (a bare `Promise.resolve()` is
  enough) parks the generator and lets that queue drain, so the code after it does see the
  children. Never branch on which of the two it is. On HYDRATION the read is misleading rather
  than empty: a child's shadow root already holds the SERVER's markup, so code that measures a
  child there gets an answer, and that answer is not evidence the client paint has happened.
- Ordering exists only between a component and the one it waits for, and there are exactly two
  reasons to wait. CAUSAL: a component written into during another component's paint updates
  after that writer, and goes on waiting for it even if something else updates it in the same
  tick. STRUCTURAL: with no writer, a component waits for every component ABOVE it that is
  also waiting to update, where above means the component whose SHADOW TREE contains this one
  (found by climbing `getRootNode().host`, through foreign shadow roots as well). So a parent
  always updates before its children, each once, whichever end of the tree the change entered
  from. It is NOT document order: two components with neither edge update in the order they
  were DIRTIED. That covers two unrelated roots, two components in the same shadow tree, and a
  component SLOTTED into another's light DOM, which has no edge to the component it is slotted
  into, only to whatever shadow tree holds them both. A loop (two components each writing a
  value that updates the other, or a paint writing its own prop a new value every time) is
  capped and ends in the same visible error an uncaught error gives.
- A `yield` of a template evaluates to the host element: ``const host = yield html`…` ``. The
  host is also on the props object, `function* ({ host })`. A yielded promise evaluates to its resolved value
  (`const data = yield fetch(...)`) and a rejected one throws at that `yield`. Any other value
  (a plain or arrow function, an `async` function, a string, an array, a thenable that is not a
  `Promise`) throws and names what a component yields. So do `yield load(…)` without the star
  and a called generator, `yield helper()`: delegate with `yield* helper()`. Yield each promise
  instead of awaiting it.
- A run of an update generator runs to completion like the component body: it may paint several
  templates in a row (a placeholder, then the result) and wait on promises between them. An
  update while a run waits does not wait for it: the old run is torn down and a new run starts,
  so the newest run always wins and a late result from a superseded run never lands.
- The component body stays parked at the `yield` of an update generator until a run of it
  FINISHES, waits included, and then continues with what that run returned. If an update
  restarts it first, the body waits for the new run. After that the body runs on while the
  update generator stays the thing `update()` re-runs, until the body yields another update
  generator or a template. So an update generator can be a step the body waits on:

  ```js
  const answered = Promise.withResolvers();
  const answer = yield function* question() {
  	yield html`<button onClick=${() => answered.resolve("yes")}>yes</button>`;
  	return yield answered.promise;
  };
  yield html`<p>you said ${answer}</p>`;
  ```

  Create the promise in the body, as here: each run is a new call, so a promise created inside
  the update generator would be a new one per update. An update generator that waits forever
  holds the body forever.
- An update generator may not yield another update generator: one level of nesting only. The
  attempt is an error OF the update generator that made it, which its own `try/catch` around
  that yield does not catch. Split a large update generator with `yield*` into plain helper
  generators instead.
- The body CAN branch: it yields whichever update generator or template fits,
  `yield isEditing ? editor : preview`. It runs once, so the choice is made once per mount. A
  choice that changes per update belongs inside one update generator, as a conditional template.
- A returned function is the cleanup: it runs on disconnect, before an update generator is
  re-run, and when the component body paints a template over a running update generator.
  `disconnectedCallback` waits a microtask and re-checks `isConnected`, so moving an element
  inside the DOM does NOT tear the component down. In the component body the return position
  holds the cleanup and nothing else: a return that is neither a function nor `undefined` is
  dropped with a warning. In an update generator, a returned function is that run's cleanup and
  the body's `yield` of it evaluates to `undefined`; any other returned value is what that
  `yield` evaluates to. Only the run the body waited on delivers its value; later runs' values
  are dropped.
- A generator torn down while it waits runs its `finally` block, and a `finally` may yield
  PROMISES: the teardown is driven to the end of the block. A new run taking the generator's
  place cuts it off with a warning: a re-mount, or for an update generator the next update,
  which starts at once, so an update generator's waiting `finally` in practice only completes on
  removal. A `finally` that yields a template or an update generator has nothing to paint into:
  that is reported through `reportError` and ends the teardown.
- On the SERVER a component runs until its first paint: yielded promises before it are awaited,
  and the code after that paint does not run there. Browser-only work (measuring, `matchMedia`,
  storage) belongs after the first paint.
- Whether an element is SERVER-RENDERED is the page's choice, never the component's: with
  vite-plugin-grundlage, `ssr` on an element turns it on and `ssr="false"` off, for everything
  inside it too. Don't add a prop or an option for it.
- An uncaught error empties the shadow tree and dispatches `grundlage-error`
  (`ComponentErrorEvent`: `error`, `tagName`; bubbles, composed, cancelable). Unless a listener
  calls `preventDefault()`, the console logs an error naming the tag and the shadow tree shows the
  error text. A `try/catch` catches what plain JavaScript lets it catch, nothing more:
  - A paint error (a wrong value in a hole) is thrown at the `yield html` that painted it, in
    the body or in an update generator. Holes before the failing one are already written, so a
    `catch` that paints nothing leaves a half-updated template; paint a fallback.
  - An error an update generator's run does not catch is thrown at the body's `yield` of it
    while the body still waits there (until the first run finishes), so a `try/catch` around
    that `yield` covers the first run, waits included.
  - After that the body has moved past that `yield` and cannot take the error back, so an
    uncaught error in a later run ends the component. An update generator that must survive an
    error on update catches it inside itself, which works on every run:

    ```js
    yield function* view() {
    	try { yield html`${formatChart(data)}`; }
    	catch { yield html`<p>chart unavailable</p>`; }
    };
    ```
- Warnings exist only in the development build, which bundlers pick through the `development`
  export condition. An exception a cleanup throws goes to `reportError`, not the console.
- In a CONTENT hole `null`, `undefined`, `false` and `true` paint nothing, since a boolean is a
  condition result, not a value. Numbers, bigints and strings always paint, `0`, `0n`,
  `NaN` and `""` included. So ``${isOpen && html`…`}`` is safe, but ``${items.length &&
  html`…`}`` writes the text `"0"` on an empty list; use a ternary for any non-boolean guard.
  An array or an ITERATOR paints as a list (see Lists and keys). An object, a function, a
  `Date`, a symbol, a `Map` or a `Set` in a content hole THROWS.
- In an ATTRIBUTE hole on an UNDECLARED name, `false`, `null` and `undefined` REMOVE the
  attribute and `true` sets it to `"true"`; a non-stringable value (object, array, function)
  is assigned as a PROPERTY instead, which is how data reaches a nested custom element.
  A name the target element DECLARES skips all of that and is assigned through that prop's
  accessor, whatever the value: `null` and `undefined` are the absence that writes the child's
  fallback back, and a value the child's function refuses warns from the PARENT's paint
  and leaves the child's previous value standing. Where the child's definition has not loaded
  yet, nothing knows the name is declared: a stringable value rides the attribute the prop
  observes, anything else lands as an own property, and both reach the store at upgrade.
- Those rules are for a value that is exactly ONE hole, which is what picks that lane, whatever
  the NAME is made of: `${name}=${value}` and `on${eventName}=${handler}` get them too. A value
  with anything else in it (`class="card ${extra}"`, `style="top:${y}px"`) is COMPOSED to a
  string instead, so that attribute is always SET and never removed: `null` and `undefined`
  contribute `""`, `false` contributes `"false"`, and an object contributes `String(value)`
  rather than reaching the property mode. Either way, a name that composes to something new
  clears the slot the old name held, listener and property mode included, before writing
  the new one.
- LIVE STATE: `value` on `<input>`/`<textarea>`, `checked` and `indeterminate` on
  `<input>`, and `selected` on `<option>` are written as the ATTRIBUTE on a binding's first commit
  (mount, server render, hydration) and as the PROPERTY on every later one. A `<textarea>` keeps
  its default in its TEXT, so its first commit writes the text instead. The attribute is the
  platform's default (`defaultValue`, `defaultChecked`), so `form.reset()` returns to the first
  painted value and `value !== defaultValue` still detects edits; the property is what is shown,
  so a state change replaces what the user typed. `null`, `undefined` and `false` empty what is
  shown (`""` or `false`) and leave the default. The change gate still compares against the last
  PAINT, not the field: an unrelated update leaves typed text alone, and writing the value the
  last paint already had writes nothing, so keep state in sync from `onInput` if a reset to that
  same value must land. Custom elements keep the ordinary attribute rules for these names. A
  composed value (`value="a ${b}"`) stays an attribute write. `<select>` has no value attribute:
  bind `selected` on each `<option>` instead (`<select value=${…}>` warns and selects nothing).
- A dynamic tag that composes to a DIFFERENT tag name swaps the element: a fresh element is
  created, attributes are copied, children are moved over, every binding anchored to it is
  re-pointed, and focus inside it is restored. Attributes survive the copy, so properties,
  listeners and declared props are re-applied; the element's identity does not survive, so a
  nested component in that position is torn down and mounted again. Composing the same name
  is a no-op.
- Events bind as `onEventName=${handler}`. The name is matched case-insensitively against the
  element's own `on*` properties, so `onClick` and `onclick` both bind `click`; a name with no
  matching property is assigned as a dead property and warns on the console. A name the target
  DECLARES is a prop first and is never matched as an event, so `once: String` is settable,
  while `on-*` is refused at define time because markup has already claimed it. Custom events
  need the `on-` prefix (`on-swatch-select=${handler}`) and keep their hyphenated name
  verbatim. The name may itself hold a hole (`on${eventName}=${handler}`), which is resolved
  from what it composes to on every paint. A quoted string (`onclick="…"`) is never a binding.
- Components paint into SHADOW DOM by default. Light-DOM selectors won't reach inside.
- Don't write literal `<!--^.^ …-->` or `<!--*.*-->` comments in template HTML: those
  prefixes are the internal markers and a collision silently misaligns hydration.
- Change detection is HASH-BASED for strings, numbers, bigints, booleans, plain objects,
  arrays, `Map`, `Set` and nested templates: mutate-then-`update()` is detected (object
  graphs are walked to a depth of 64). Class instances, `Date`, typed arrays and functions
  are compared by REFERENCE identity, so mutating one in place reads as unchanged and is
  skipped. Pass plain data, or replace the reference to signal a change. A declared prop is
  the one place that does not skip: `el.items.push(x)` alone does not trigger an update, but
  `el.items = el.items` does, because a value that could have been mutated behind its
  reference is never called unchanged.
  It lands on the next paint from any cause, where these hashes pick the new contents up.
- A dynamic `<style>` is fast when every `${…}` sits in a declaration VALUE: the mounted (and
  server-rendered) sheet text carries the real literal values, and every later update is a
  `setProperty` on this element's OWN CSSOM sheet, never a reparse, never a write to the
  host. Each instance owns a private sheet, so duplicates never collide. Structural holes
  (selector, property name, at-rule prelude), the same holed property declared twice in one
  block, an ambiguous `!important`, and a sheet the browser parses differently than the
  library expects (e.g. it drops a rule it can't parse) fall back to a full text rewrite that is
  always correct, just slower. Consequences: a runtime value the browser rejects (including
  one that smuggles `;` or `!important`) is dropped and the PREVIOUS value stays, a static
  `!important` is preserved as CSSOM priority, a CSS-wide keyword
  (`inherit`/`initial`/`unset`/`revert`) takes its normal effect, and serialized output
  (`getHTML`) reflects the last full-text write, not later CSSOM updates.
- Declare inputs in `component(gen, { props })` and read them off the object the component body
  and its update generators receive. Don't read attributes directly: they're strings, they skip
  the parsing, defaults and refusal the schema gives, and an undeclared attribute does not
  trigger an update.
- The props object IS the store, so it is live rather than a snapshot: a value read after a
  yielded promise settles is current rather than the one the run started with. WHERE YOU
  DESTRUCTURE therefore decides what you get, and this is the most common mistake. The component
  body runs ONCE, so `component(function* ({ label }) …)` freezes `label` at mount. That is
  right for an initial value or a mount-time branch, WRONG for anything an update generator
  paints. An update generator runs per update, so `yield function* view({ label }) …` is live,
  and so is reading `componentProps.label` off the object. `{ ...componentProps }` is how you
  take a deliberate snapshot, by the language's own rule. The object is handed out READONLY:
  writing to it would move a value nothing parsed, reflected or scheduled on.
  `componentProps.host.count = 5` is the spelling that does all three, and it is the same one an
  outside caller uses (`element.count = 5`).
- `load` reuses the server's result only while hydrating and runs the fetcher everywhere else;
  don't add a fetch-once cache around it.
- TypeScript only: a yielded promise evaluates to `any`, because one generator has one resume
  type for all of its yields. Annotate the binding, `const user: User = yield fetchUser(id)`,
  or delegate to a typed helper whose `yield*` returns `T`:

  ```typescript
  function* awaited<T>(promise: Promise<T>): Generator<Promise<T>, T, T> {
  	return yield promise;
  }
  const user = yield* awaited(fetchUser(id)); // User
  ```

  `yield* load(() => fetchUser(id))` is typed the same way, by its fetcher.
- TypeScript only: a schema hoisted out of the `component(…)` call needs `satisfies Schema`.
  Inline, `{ count: [Number, 0] }` is contextually typed; hoisted, `[Number, 0]` widens to
  `(NumberConstructor | number)[]` and stops being a valid entry. A function entry also needs
  its parameter annotated, `[(incoming: unknown) => …, fallback]`, because an entry may be a
  function or one of four constructors and all five are callable. An update generator or
  `yield*` helper typed by hand annotates as `Generator<YieldableValue>`, not bare `Generator`,
  and takes the SHAPE it reads (`{ host: BaseComponent; readonly userId: string | undefined }`),
  never `ComponentProps<typeof someSchema>`: that type claims the host carries those accessors,
  and a delegating parent's host carries its own instead. The component generator's return
  position is `Cleanup | void` (`Cleanup` is exported), so a wrong return is a compile error,
  not a silent drop. An update generator's return position is `unknown` (the exported
  `UpdateGenerator` type), since it returns a value to the body; its `yield` in the body
  evaluates to `any`, like a promise's.
- Form components: `component(gen, { formAssociated: true })` re-dispatches the four form
  callbacks as host events `form-associated` `{form}`, `form-disabled` `{disabled}`,
  `form-reset` (no detail) and `form-state-restore` `{state, mode}`, bindable declaratively
  as `on-form-*` on the host `<template>`.
